content: Hypertension, also known as high blood pressure, is a significant risk factor for cardiovascular disease and a major public health concern. The prevalence of hypertension has increased in the United States due to a change in diagnostic thresholds, with the previous cutoff of 140/90 mmHg (as per the 2003 JNC 7 guidelines) being lowered to 130/80 mmHg. Hypertension is a leading cause of mortality worldwide, and more than half of hypertensive patients are unaware of their condition. Even among those diagnosed, many do not adhere to prescribed medications. The new guidelines recommend averaging blood pressure readings from at least two office visits. Home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) are superior to office or clinic readings for identifying masked hypertension or white coat hypertension. Hypertension was first identified in 1896 by Scipione Riva-Rocci, an Italian physician, following the invention of the mercury sphygmomanometer. In 1905, Nikolai Korotkoff, a Russian physician, described the sounds heard during cuff deflation. Between 1910 and 1914, the terms essential hypertension and malignant hypertension were introduced. Hypertension is classified into two main categories based on the presence of underlying disorders: 1. Chronic hypertension (primary or essential hypertension): This accounts for 90-95% of cases and is characterized by a gradual rise in blood pressure. Contributing factors include environmental exposures (e.g., weight gain, high-sodium diet, reduced physical activity, excessive alcohol consumption), family history, and lifestyle changes. 2. Secondary hypertension: This accounts for 5% of cases and is caused by underlying conditions such as: Pheochromocytoma (sudden BP spikes with pallor and dizziness) Obstructive sleep apnea (snoring, hypersomnolence) Chronic kidney disease (e.g., due to post-renal urinary tract obstruction) Primary aldosteronism or renovascular disease (hypokalemia, muscle cramps, weakness) Hyperthyroidism (weight loss, palpitations, heat intolerance) Cushing syndrome (central obesity, facial rounding, easy bruising) Medication or substance use (e.g., NSAIDs, alcohol, cocaine, amphetamines) Coarctation of the aorta (residual hypertension post-repair) Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure that remains above target levels despite the concurrent use of three antihypertensive drugs, including a long-acting calcium channel blocker, an ACE inhibitor or ARB, and a diuretic. Refractory hypertension refers to cases unresponsive to at least five classes of antihypertensive medications. The 2017 ACC/AHA guidelines classify hypertension into two stages based on severity. The pathophysiology of hypertension involves dysfunction in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), natriuretic peptides, the endothelium, the sympathetic nervous system, and the immune system. Genetic factors, including polygenic and monogenic mutations, also play a role. Environmental factors such as obesity, high sodium intake, low potassium intake, and physical inactivity are significant contributors. Hypertension is more prevalent among older adults, males, and individuals of Black, Asian, or Hispanic descent. Common risk factors include diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, obesity, low socioeconomic status, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, obstructive sleep apnea, and psychological stress. Patients with primary hypertension are typically asymptomatic, while secondary hypertension may present with symptoms such as palpitations, headaches, sweating, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, muscle cramps, or skin lesions. Physical examination findings in secondary hypertension may include arterial bruits, irregular pulses, tachycardia, abdominal masses, skin changes (e.g., striae, pallor), central obesity, moon face, or orthostatic hypotension. Diagnostic evaluation includes accurate blood pressure measurement, cardiovascular risk assessment, and investigation for secondary causes. Laboratory tests include fasting blood sugar, complete blood count, lipid profile, serum creatinine with eGFR, serum electrolytes, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and urinalysis. Optional tests include uric acid and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio. Imaging studies such as ECG, chest X-ray, echocardiography, CT, or MRI may be used to assess complications or underlying causes. Treatment involves lifestyle modifications and pharmacological therapy. First-line medications include calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and thiazide-like diuretics. Beta-blockers are preferred in cases of angina or heart failure. Resistant hypertension may require additional agents such as spironolactone, hydralazine, or minoxidil. Surgical interventions may be necessary for secondary hypertension caused by conditions like coarctation of the aorta or primary aldosteronism. Preventive measures include weight loss, a healthy diet (rich in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy), reduced sodium intake, increased potassium intake, regular physical activity, and limited alcohol consumption. Patients diagnosed with hypertension should be monitored monthly to evaluate medication adherence and treatment response. Untreated hypertension can lead to severe complications, including myocardial infarction, stroke, end-stage renal disease, and death.
